publication-005.text:
USAID
USAID
FROM THE AMERICAN PEOPLE
FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY
INFORMATION MEMO FOR ADMINISTRATOR POWER
Date:
June 2, 2022
From:
Vera Zakem, Senior Technology and Democracy Advisor, DDI/DRG
Subject:
USAID Initial Response to Address Mis/Dis/Mal-Information
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Mis/Dis/Mal-Information (MDM)' has become a pervasive problem for USAID, the
broader U.S. government (USG), and the world, affecting our partners, and posing
significant risk to USAID and its staff, especially in the field. This challenge and the
information environment is rapidly evolving, and requires continuous assessment of how
to best respond to it, and strengthen its integrity and resiliency.
• While USAID is seeking to find appropriate, contextualized answers, we also recognize
that this challenge is global, and is scaling faster than we can understand. While we aim
to repair and reinforce resiliencethose elements in of our society and at USAID from this
challenge, we need to manage MDM's disruptions and impacts on society, our partners,
the Agency and USG's goals, and our staff. Because this impacts all sectors of the
Agency, a whole-of-Agency response is required.
• This memo includes specific actions, in response to the is a follow up to the previous
memo that outlined some of the key cases of MDM at USAID. It proposes concrete next
steps to address this challenge for USAID.
BACKGROUND:
• In response to this ongoing challenge, on May 25th, DDI/DRG conducted a strategic
planning workshop with approximately 50 participants from each of the regional bureaus,
CPS, PPL and DDI. Prior to the workshop, DDI/DRG conducted an agency-wide survey
to gather feedback from USAID/Washington and Missions that received over 100
responses. Below are the key takeaways:
• The need to identify, share, strengthen, and evaluate the impact programming:
USAID requires an Agency-wide approach to address disinformation related challenges.
1 While USAID has addressed this challenge as MDM, the USG interagency commonly refers to it as
information integrity and resilience. The threats associated with it are grouped under "information
manipulation."

Current approaches across the Agency lack an understanding of the impact that our
efforts have on strengthening the resilience of the information and media environment in
order to reduce the damaging effects of MDM. In addition, a full lack of understanding
exists on various approaches undertaken by USAID's Bureaus and OUs to address this
challenge.
• The need to assess, identify, and clarify roles, responsibilities, and response
mechanisms: Roles, responsibilities, and response mechanisms are largely undefined
both within respective B/IOs as well as Agency wide. While some B/IOs are leaning
forward to program and measure the impact of the programs in this space (for example,
DRG or GH on public health messaging), other B/IOs require deeper understanding of
how MDM impacts their work as well as programming options and best practices to
address it. Furthermore, there is insufficient research, monitoring and evaluation, and
programmatic approaches to address this challenge in the Global South. While the scope
of this challenge is truly global, USAID is uniquely positioned to fill this gap, given our
global presence and work in diverse sectors.
• The need to assess our operations in order to respond to reputational and security
risks: Information manipulation affects USAID's reputation and security as well as those
of its staff and implementing partners. USAID operates in countries where the USG has
not mapped out the information environment landscape nor assessed the risks MDM may
pose to its operations. USAID lacks communication guidance on how to message and
communicate about MDM with our missions, implementing partners, adn civil society.
Further, USAID lacks clear operational guidance on how to assess impact and report an
MDM incident and respond effectively. A solution would entail clarifying USAID's
policies, organizational structures, training, resources, budget, and personnel to document
these instances and to respond when a potentially harmful incident of MDM threatens.
• The need to strengthen interagency coordination: USAID could benefit from more
intentional interagency coordination both in DC and in the field, to leverage resources
within the USG in order to strengthen the integrity of the information environment.
USAID employees are not systematically made aware of the tools available across the
USG that may help them in their response. Moving forward, USAID has an opportunity
to influence the USG interagency to develop strategy and policy, supported by our
programs to address this challenge. In addition, USAID may suggest that the USG
interagency revisit lessons learned from the last two decades of our efforts in
counterterrorism and counter violent extremism, and the coordination mechanisms that
were operationalized to advance that craft across the USG.
2

• The need for localized and contextual solutions to understand the information and
media environment: Addressing MDM requires understanding of local cultures, people,
and languages. Given USAID's global footprint and partnerships with civil society,
media, and local population, and the understanding of the impact that MDM has on local
populations and movements, USAID has a substantial comparative advantage to bring
these insights both to the interagency and to its partnership with the tech sector.
However, to date, threat actor based approaches, also known as the "supply side" of
MDM, have dominated USG discussions and national security agenda.
• The need to strengthen our relationship with the tech sector: USAID should solidify
and expand partnerships with both digital platforms and emerging technologies to counter
MDM in order to establish direct communication on MDM-related content moderation
decisions, and advocate for greater transparency of content moderation processes that
affect USAID. To facilitate this engagement, USAID's missions could partner with
digital platforms and emerging technologies, particularly in places where these
companies lack significant local presence or operations. Moreover, USAID has a unique
opportunity to work with the tech sector to build an affirmative agenda that includes
creating resilience mechanisms to strengthen the information environment such as media,
digital literacy, and cyber hygiene trainings, and ways for local media and civil society to
report disinformation campaigns.
NEXT STEPS:
To address and accelerate mitigation strategies, on behalf of the DRG Center, I will be leading
this initiative. To do so, I will leverage DRG's Information Domain Task Team (IDTT), with
cross-agency representation to stand up a broader body, with participation from senior leadership
at the DAA / Director level to achieve the following objectives in the initial 60 to 90 days, and
build on the existing body of work. We will create outcome-oriented sub-working groups to lead
on issues identified in this memo in order to align various Agency activities and efforts with
Agency, interagency, and Administration strategic priorities:
Defining the Problem
• Agree upon a definition to categorize this challenge that is consistent with the USG
interagency, and a definition that minimizes reputational and security risk to USAID.
Finalize Problem/Needs Assessment
• Assess the best way to prioritize identified gaps;
Develop coordinated whole-of-Agency Response
• Develop an interim framework document to address the challenge and provide guidance
to USAID Missions and B/IOs. This framework document will align USAID's mission
3

and goals against proposed strategic priorities across operational, programmatic, and
multi-sector engagement lines of effort in order to address MDM gaps and challenges for
the Agency, including identification of a few select countries to pilot specific our efforts;
• Expand Programmatic Responses:
• Develop the strategic objectives for USAID's response to this challenge;
• Conduct a scoping of existing programs that are directly/indirectly addressing
MDM and establish mechanisms to share best practices;
• Identify gaps in programming, identify opportunities for innovation such as Grand
Challenges or other approaches;
• Reform USAID Operations:
Through Agency consultations and co-led with PPL, LPA, SEC and HCTM
among others, identify operational changes to address reputational, security risk,
and employee resilience;
• Establish clear strategic communication guidelines, in collaboration with LPA;
• Strengthen partnerships and coordination:
• Expand and solidify a relationship with the technology sector, both digital
platforms and emerging technologies, including on content moderation and
strengthening resilience of the information environment;
• Expand USAID's relationship with the USG interagency, including the NSC,
DOD, State, and other equities;
Establish a cross-sector community of practice with implementing partners/NGO/
academia/think tanks to elevate and share MDM challenges, identify new partners
and share best practices in the field;
• Long Term Priorities
• Explore and assess longterm Agency requirements to address disinformation
related challenges, including organizational structure, policy, resourcing,
processing, and operational response;
• Continue to document lessons learned and incorporate Agency's best practices to
respond to disinformation in the Year of Action, leading up to the next Summit
for Democracy.
• Assess continuous research and analysis needs to meet this challenge.
• Promote a whole-of-community approach to help empower citizens and civil
society to address MDM, and increase social capital.
Organization
4

This initiative will elevate the DRG-led IDTT, with Agency-wide representation and include
senior leadership participation at the DAA level to action the deliverables identified above. We
will meet with senior level leadership on a monthly basis and at the working level on a biweekly
basis.

publication-003.text:
INFORMATION MEMO FOR ADMINISTRATOR POWER
Date:
February 22, 2022
From:
Sophia Lalani, Senior National Security Advisor, A/AID
CC:
Gideon Maltz, Sonali Korde, Colin Thomas-Jensen
Subject:
USAID's Response to Disinformation Across Bureaus
Administrator,
In response to your request to better understand the scope of disinformation and USAID's
response to disinformation in areas where USAID works, we commissioned four case studies to
describe four different types of disinformation environments USAID faces: Ethiopia
(state-sponsored disinformation and hate speech); Nepal (PRC influenced propaganda against
U.S. development programs); Central Asia (disinformation targeting USAID employees) and
Ukraine (Russian anti-West, anti-NATO disinformation). These are attached as tabs. While
these are not exhaustive, they provide illustrative examples of the types of disinformation in the
field and a review of USAID's response and capabilities.
USAID programs to counter mis/dis/malinformation (MDM) include financial support for media
and digital internet literacy, financial support to organizations that conduct fact checking
mechanisms, and training and equipment to increase quality journalism. Elements of
counter-disinformation programming also feature in our work across other sectors, for example
USAID provides grants to health organizations to conduct public health campaigns combatting
COVID-19 disinformation, financial support to organizations conducting gender and social
media monitoring, among other approaches. Because USAID has been in Ukraine for 30 years,
there is some data regarding the effectiveness of USAID programming there, which found
significant increases in the number of respondents able to identify the difference between true
and false information. However, little survey data regarding USAID program effectiveness is
available for the other case studies.
Gaps in USAID and USG Approach to Disinformation: Our scoping exercise has revealed
several gaps in the USG and USAID's approach to disinformation. First, we are not sharing
examples of disinformation or information manipulation - or potential responses - across the
agency. Bureaus and missions are developing ad hoc solutions, without systematically sharing
best practices, data, or analytics. In addition, it is not clear if all Missions are prepared and
trained on responding to MDM. Nor do we have a clear method for Missions to report MDM
against our work or staff. Across the USG no one entity owns the disinformation problem set:
DHS, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), DOJ, DOD, the
FBI, ODNI, and the broader intelligence community have their own efforts to identify, expose,
and even carry out punitive measures (such as OFAC sanctions against Russian individuals
believed to be behind the 2016 presidential elections interference). Domestic agencies
including CISA, the Census Bureau, and the CDC analyze disinformation that undermines their

work. Meanwhile the Federal research community including Sandia National Laboratories,
DARPA, and the National Science Foundation are supporting a range of related projects related
to identifying information manipulation. The interagency's struggle to assess, plan for, and
counter Russian disinformation targeting Ukraine or Government of Ethiopia's efforts to incite
violence against Tigrayans provide current examples of how the lack of coordination prevents
the USG from being postured to effectively address national security risks of disinformation.
Interagency engagement : USAID attends the Information Integrity and Resilience IPC, which
has met biweekly since May 2021 and is developing a National Security Memorandum on how
to respond to disinformation; this will go to Deputies on March 1. Unfortunately, most of the
discussion to date has focused on the domestic threat and operational response efforts, leaving
us very light on strategy for the international aspects of disinformation. While there has been
agreement that better interagency coordination is needed, meetings have bogged down in
disagreement over which agency controls what: ODNI and DOJ want the IC to avoid any role
when purely domestic actors engage in disinformation, and while NSC would like State's Global
Engagement Center to take on a coordinating role, USAID believes it should co-own foreign
disinformation efforts because it overwhelmingly owns the relevant programming by dollar
amount, and its field presence allows for early warning of disinformation campaigns. No
concrete alternatives have been offered to overcome the impasse.
Next Steps: DDI/DRG has taken the closest thing to an overall lead role within the Agency in
coordination with the missions. They published a Disinformation Primer and assembled the
Information Domain Task team Disinformation task team that gathers 20 individuals from various
bureaus and technical offices to discuss NSC updates, USG policy and research development,
multilateral updates (e.g. WHO infodemic updates), and interagency coordination.
The team appreciates any feedback or steers on the suggested path forward on both
intra-Agency and interagency next steps. One next step we are considering is to formalize this
team and add representation from additional offices or bureaus. This task team would complete
a stock taking of all USAID assets, capabilities and gaps. As one option, we could create a
Sector Council on disinformation that DRG could co-chair with PPL to encourage coordination
across the Agency. We are also considering drafting a USAID strategy on MDM, which currently
does not exist. DAA Johnny Walsh has indicated that the first Summit for Democracy featured
little direct focus on disinformation, and it would be reasonable to look at ways to incorporate it
in deliverables this year and/or Year of Action work with partners. The team is in the early
stages of refining USAID capabilities and responses and crafting USAID's role within any
interagency coordination process, and will refine these deliverables as we develop and
strengthen the task team.
Information Memos:
Info Memo: Disinformation and Programming in Ethiopia
Info Memo: Disinformation and Programming in Ukraine
Info Memo: Disinformation and Programming in Central Asia
Info Memo: Disinformation and Programming in Nepal
USAID Disinformation Primer (DRG Center)

FROM THE AMERICAN PEOPLE
INFORMATION MEMO FOR ADMINISTRATOR POWER
Date:
February 17, 2022
From:
Jonathan Dworken, AFR/EA and Brittany Brown, CPS/OTI
Subject:
Ethiopia Mis/Disinformation
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• (SBU) The conflict in northern Ethiopia, exacerbated by government suppression of
intormation, is the frontline of the mis/disinformation battlefield.
• A "war of narratives" playing out on social media and state-owned media was propagated
with targeted mis/disinformation in Ethiopia.
• (SBU) Throughout the conflict, Ethiopian public opinion of the United States has
drastically declined. Through a barrage of social media and other means, the Government
of Ethiopia (GOE) took deliberate efforts to (1) discredit and undermine the U.S.
government's (USG) calls for a ceasefire, (2) counter GOE embarrassment resulting from
a more aggressive USG posture, (3) reduce credibility of USG efforts to identify
atrocities and prevent further violence, and (4) inflame pre-existing perceptions of U.S.
bias in favor of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Pro-government media
posts have also made claims that USAID and other donors are using humanitarian
assistance as political leverage (going insofar as claiming humanitarians facilitate arms
smuggling to support one party to the conflict). As a result of President Biden's recent
call to Prime Minister Abiy, the perception of a constructive USG role has improved.
• Mis/disinformation within Ethiopia (via social media and government communications)
has also been used effectively to change internal political and ethnic power dynamics.
Ethnic mis/disinformation has been particularly effective and has served to jeopardize the
fragile status quo that exists in this ethnic federation.
• (SBU) USAID, and the Department of State based on a National Security Council (NSC)
request, have worked to address and monitor the impact of mis/disinformation in Ethiopia
(including its effect on furthering intercommunal conflict).
BACKGROUND:
(SBU) Biased information, intercommunal hate speech, and mis/disinformation
undermine the prospect for national consensus, peace, and good governance in Ethiopia. In
particular, divisive information, frequently elevated by social media algorithms, is deepening
social and political polarization and sparking violence in communities with historical grievances.
The effect of these is particularly acute and visible in the context of the conflict in Northern
Ethiopia, where disinformation (accompanied by a communications blackout and restricted
access to Tigray) has led to competing narratives by the conflicting parties, including allegations
of war crimes, atrocities, genocide, and conflict progression. Coordinated amplification of
targeted (competing) narratives via Tweets addressing the Tigray conflict (both supporting and
opposing Ethiopia's government) led to confusion and continues to undermine efforts for peace.
(SBU) The GOE regularly promoted disinformation on social media to undermine voices
calling for dialogue. In November 2021, prominent Prosperity Party member and State Minister
[ February 17, 2022] 1/13

of Peace Taye Dendea Aredo alleged on Facebook that USAID was leaving Ethiopia due to the
GoE's refusal to open the Humera corridor (Tab 1-A). He further argued that USAID has been in
Ethiopia but "literally changed nothing." Social media posts have also used disinformation to
further a narrative that USAID's humanitarian assistance in northern Ethiopia is political in
nature and gone insofar as to claim that humanitarians facilitate arms smuggling to one party to
the conflict - the TPLF (Tab 1-B, C, D).
(SBU) Additionally, there is a diaspora-driven social media campaign to counter alleged
Western government bias against the GOE. Ethiopia's sizable diasporaboth in the United
States and around the worldplays a significant role in the information space, such as in
propagating misinformation, disinformation, and mal-information (MDM) within Ethiopia. The
combined use of satellite television stations and social media platforms by some individuals
within the diaspora to spread hate speech is one of the main drivers of harmful narratives in
Ethiopia. Some members of the diaspora also serve as major financial and moral supporters of
Ethiopian-run television stations that are key propagators of hate speech in the country. Efforts to
identify a large portion of MDM as it occurs struggle to trace MDM as it spreads through
Ethiopia's dozens of languages.
The #NoMore campaign, an online project started within the global Ethiopian diaspora in
the second half of 2021, is a movement to counter alleged foreign interference in the internal
affairs of Ethiopia and alleged intentional dissemination of false information regarding the
conflict in Northern Ethiopia. The campaign accuses the USG of backing the TPLF and has
organized demonstrations in the United States, Canada, and around the globe. According to the
State Department's Global Engagement Center (GEC) reports, U.S. Embassy posts receiving the
most engagement were those specifically commenting on the deterioration of Ethiopia's security
environment and urging U.S. citizens to leave. The most popular responses to these posts
conveyed sentiments of betrayal by the USG, suggesting the USG was favoring the TPLF and
engaging in colonialist practices. Articles in state-owned media outlets discussing the #NoMore
campaign specifically referenced you as Administrator (Tab 1-E).
(SBU) With respect to good governance, one observed trend according to GEC reports is
of posts with high co-tweet counts that characterize international involvement in the ongoing
crisis in Tigray as a threat to Ethiopian sovereignty, including through the use of hashtags such as
#DemocracyShallWin.
(SBU) USAID Programming to Counter Mis/disinformation in Ethiopia:
In 2021, the NSC tasked the interagency to create an interagency action plan, with
top-line messages, specific goals, and accompanying lines of effort, for mitigating hate speech
(and disinformation) during the sensitive election and post-election period (Note: the Ethiopian
presidential election happened in several rounds starting in summer 2021), including amplifying
credible local voices promoting peace, cohesion, and reconciliation and coordinating with
like-minded international partners. The plan included a human rights analysis of Ethiopia's Hate
Speech and Disinformation Prevention and Suppression Proclamation enacted in 2020 and
provided recommended action for the USG to pursue both through diplomacy and through
programming. In August 2021, a Strategic Communications and Outreach Plan developed for
review by the NSC identified priority actions, including combating online hate speech and
dis/misinformation that hardened ethnic divisions among Ethiopians and entrenched the crisis.
Megatalkers were also developed and agreed upon.
[February 17, 2022] 2/13

USAID is countering mis/disinformation (and hate speech) in Ethiopia, contributing
programming to various lines of effort within the aforementioned interagency action plan. In
summary:
• USAID's Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) currently has about 15 activities
addressing mis/disinformation (and hate speech) in Ethiopia. Designed to better
understand where online hate speech translates into offline violence and supporting
locally led actors and initiatives to mitigate such violence, these activities partner with
local media outlets, media professionals, community radios, youth, government officials,
and civil-society organizations nationally. OTI equips and networks key stakeholders to
produce accurate, fact-checked, and unbiased information in an accessible manner and
supports activities to limit the influence of mis/disinformation and hate speech from
triggering conflict. To date, OTI has supported about 83 radio shows; fact-checked over
390 news pieces; trained 1,121 influencers (mostly youth); and worked with about 83
media outlets. Additional activities are under development.
To better understand the relationships among mis/disinformation, good governance, and
conflict mitigation, OTI also supports a local organization in producing biweekly social
media monitoring reports. These media monitoring reports contribute to additional
USAID and USAID partner analysis into the nexus and dynamics of online and
conventional media rhetoric and offline acts of intercommunal violence. The reports are
used to build interagency understanding on a fast-moving and highly contentious problem
set. OTI shares them with GEC/State Department who are in process of sharing them
with Big Tech (Twitter, Facebook, YouTube) to flag false content or hate speech on their
respective platforms. Local civil-society organizations, academics, think tanks, and media
organizations within Ethiopia also use them to raise awareness about MDM and build
media literacy.
• USAID/Ethiopia/Office of Democracy and Governance also supports countering
mis/disinformation through several programs that strengthen fact-checking, train
journalists and media houses on identifying and reporting on disinformation, and support
entities that produce reports assessing the scope and impact of disinformation. In
addition, USAID/Ethiopia supports training of journalists and media houses in reporting
on conflict and human rights issues, which includes support for content creation around
investigations and news stories on human rights and gender-informed conflict-mitigation
reports. USAID/Ethiopia also provides support for development of public media
programming around hate speech and disinformation.
Lessons Learned:
USAID has derived a number of lessons learned from its activities that are affecting
current and future programming. Of note, there is a conflict-sensitive reporting knowledge gap
among media professionals in Ethiopia as they need to better understand how their reporting can
inadvertently trigger violence and how they can mitigate against this; fact-checking programs
struggle to securing advertising over concerns with being associated with "sensitive" programs;
and there are benefits to linking youth in USAID-funded activities who have expressed an
[February 17, 2022] 3/13

interest in gaining fact-checking experience/knowledge to other USAID partners who have
technical expertise in fact-checking to support the development of those skills among youth.
NEXT STEPS:
• USAID will continue to implement activities countering mis/disinformation (and hate
speech) in Ethiopia, contributing to various lines of effort within the aforementioned
interagency action plan. Note that USAID does not provide messaging guidance to our
partners, and the efforts are not aimed at countering a particular type of
mis/disinformation (e.g., disinformation related to USG assistance).
• USAID also plans to explore the nexus of online rhetoric and offline violence through
potential future programming to support better research and early action in this space.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• (U) The Kremlin has stepped up its malign information operations in Ukraine as tensions
have increased. While spending is not broken down per country, the Government of
Russia plans to spend $2.88 billion from 2021-2025 to expand the global reach of RT,

• (U) USAID/Ukraine's media-related programs total $60 million and assist partners to
address disinformation by augmenting high-quality, independent media production
capacity and providing content monitoring and analysis support. They could expand or
pivot as the situation warrants, including to address information manipulation.
BACKGROUND:
(U) Information Landscape in Ukraine. The Kremlin has been ramping up its
disinformation offensive in Ukraine in the past few months, using Russian state-owned
broadcasters and trolls on social media platforms to portray the West as the aggressor and the
government in Kyiv as its puppet. The Government of Ukraine (GoU) has taken steps to counter
Kremlin-sponsored disinformation, including banning several Kremlin-linked media outlets and
establishing two new centers to combat disinformation. At the same time, the GoU has been
increasing pressure on independent media outlets in the past few months, including threats of
criminal prosecution against media outlets and journalists critical of the GoU and underfunding
the public service broadcaster in spite of legal requirements, while a bill threatening media
independence has been registered and awaits review by parliament. See Tab 1 for more details.
(SBU) USAID's Media and Information Integrity Support in Ukraine. Globally,
USAID views the challenge of information manipulation through a development lens and thus
approaches it as an information integrity issue, as well as a cross-sectoral issue that affects other
development goals, including economic growth, health, and the environment. Programs generally
aim to increase resilience in the media and information space, rather than engage in
information/psychological operations or strategic communications to amplify U.S. foreign policy
narratives, which are in the purview of the Department of Defense and Department of State,
respectively. For more information, see Tab 2.
(SBU) USAID's support to independent media development in Ukraine in the past 30
years has helped advance major successes in the information space, including strengthening
plurality and diversity of new, independent media sources; creating strong local media support
organizations that conduct expert polling and media monitoring and mentor other burgeoning
organizations in the region, such as in Belarus; and supporting new legal reforms related to the

media sector, including the key reform of Ukraine's National Public Service Broadcaster
(UA:PBC) and the law on access to public information.
(U) USAID/Ukraine's Media Program in Ukraine (MPU) aims to strengthen the role of
media in democratic processes in Ukraine and expand citizens' access to high-quality
information to counter malign influence and support European integration. Last year, an online
comedy show that debunks disinformation, Newspalm, reached 2 million views, was picked up
by 14 regional TV channels across the country, and won accolades from Ukrainian public
figures. In another example, an MPU-supported blogger who covers disinformation reached 1.3
million views on TikTok and 1.8 million on YouTube. Her most popular video was about a newly
created pro-Russian TV Channel that has the same hosts, guests, narratives, and management as
recently GOU-blocked channels. The most liked comment on her channel was "Now we know
more about information bubbles, political manipulations, and the life of journalists from the
inside. Your account is a jewel in the media sphere." In comparison, and to demonstrate what
USAID's partners are up against, Anatoly Shariy, a popular pro-Kremlin blogger in Ukraine
known for xenophobic rhetoric, receives on average 1 million views per video on YouTube and
TikTok, and some of his videos on TikTok have received as many as 5 million views.
(SBU)-USAID/Ukraine's Transformation Communications Activity, in collaboration with
USAID/Office of Transition Initiatives' (OTI) Ukraine Confidence Building Initiative, supports
the creation of social impact entertainment that serves as an alternative to Kremlin-backed

pro-Kremlin views. Analysis of these debates over time suggests that Kremlin-supported

advance the GoU's partnerships with civil-society organizations (CSOs) and its capacity to

Tab 1-Disinformation Landscape and Low Levels of Trust in Media in Ukraine
(U) Ukraine is fighting against Kremlin hybrid warfare, political interference, and
disinformation aimed at undermining Ukraine's cybersecurity, infrastructure, and governance.
Out of the more than 13,500 cases about Kremlin-sponsored disinformation campaigns that the
European Union's (EU) European External Action Service has cataloged, exposed, and debunked
since 2015, Ukraine is mentioned in nearly 40 percent. The most prevalent and dangerous myths
that the Kremlin promotes about Ukraine include anti-Western narratives, such as that the North
Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is "aggressive" and inflames tensions, that Ukraine
continues to commit atrocities and human rights violations in the east against Russian-speaking
populations, and that the West and the EU have abandoned Ukraine. A recent report from the
Center for European Policy Analysis noted that domestically, the Government of Russia is
preparing Russians for the prospect of imminent war using Russian state media, propagandists,
and politicians, while trolls and bots are increasingly amplifying both domestic and international
messaging on social media. Russian international broadcasting entity RT has also been
publishing more op-eds from Western academics willing to make arguments that align with
Kremlin-supported talking points and narratives. Last year, the Government of Russia
announced plans to spend $2.88 billion from 2021-2025, with about $450 million for 2021 alone,
to increase the reach of broadcasting entities RT, Rossiya Segodnya, and Sputnik.
(U) Ukraine is taking steps to counter Kremlin-sponsored disinformation. Earlier this
year, the Zelenskyy administration banned a number of Kremlin-linked media outlets from
responding to Russian aggression in the information arena. The GoU has created two new
organizations to combat disinformation: the Center for Countering Disinformation within the
National Security and Defense Council, and the Ministry of Culture and Information Policy's
Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security.
(SBU) At the same time, the president's office has been increasing pressure on
independent media outlets in the past few months, including: pressure on publication owners to
not publish stories about corruption among some political and financial elites; unrealistic
demands to political talk shows for interviews/coverage, including on the editorially independent
public service broadcaster; attempts to cancel the screening of a documentary film on
Zelenskyy's offshore businesses revealed in the recent Pandora Papers leaks; and threats of
criminal prosecution against media outlets and journalists who are critical of the GoU. A bill
threatening media independence has also been registered and awaits review by parliament.
Finally, the government is seeking to expand funding for state media to amplify its message,
while decreasing funding for the public service broadcaster, which the government has
consistently underfunded since its founding in 2017 in spite of legal funding requirements.
(U) Pressure on the information landscape from without and within may be helping to
raise distrust of Ukrainians toward all media. A recent survey in Ukraine suggests trust in
Russian media is virtually nonexistent, while citizens' trust of domestic media is also low.
According to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology survey conducted by telephone in
December 2021, 32 percent of Ukrainians trusted Ukrainian media, compared to 30 percent in
December 2020, and 39 percent said they did not trust Ukrainian media, compared to 43 percent
in 2020. At the same time, just 3 percent trusted Russian media, compared to 4 percent in 2020,
and 79 percent distrusted Russian media, up 1 percent from 2020. The highest overall media trust

PROGRAM'S COUNTER
DISINFORMATION EFFORTS
USAID/OTI's Ukraine program uses a multifaceted approach to countering disinformation by focusing on
addressing the harms from hostile state information operations aimed at stoking tensions and
undermining democracy. This approach includes: support for the production of creative content that
tackle important macro narratives being pushed by the Kremlin and Kremlin-aligned media; technical and
strategic assistance to the Government of Ukraine (GOU) on approaches to countering disinformation;
support for local media outlets and civil society organizations in vulnerable regions of Ukraine to
improve the quality of their locally relevant, factual content. Underpinning these approaches are ongoing
research and close coordination with other USAID programs, the Embassy Public Affairs Section, DOD,
and other key donors such as the UK and EU.
NARRATIVES & CREATIVE CONTENT
PROBLEM/OPPORTUNITY
Combined with the targeted, specific media
narratives about how bad things are in
Ukraine, the Kremlin also relies on its film,
TV, and music industry to use soft power that
promotes the Kremlin worldview. Oftentimes
this content has high production value and
slick promotion - appealing to many
Ukrainians and others in the former Soviet
region. This creates an opportunity to develop
quality content that challenges Kremlin
narratives and highlights an accurate portrayal
of Ukraine and Euro-Atlantic values.
RESPONSE
On the broadest scale, OTI works on supporting
creative content that promotes Euro-Atlantic values
and helps reinforce Ukraine's pluralistic national
identity, especially amongst audiences who are most
vulnerable to Kremlin-backed disinformation efforts.
This includes populations living in the
non-government controlled areas (NGCA's) of
Donbas and occupied Crimea as well as audiences in
southern and eastern Ukraine. Support consists of
full content production, marketing and promotion,
and underwriting script development and pilot
episodes.
• High Quality Social Impact Content: The flagship approach through which OTI identifies content to
support is through the PitchUA process. PitchUA, created and designed by OTI, is an open call for
Ukrainian creatives to pitch their concepts in line with themes that advance the overall objective of a
unified, stable, and democratic Ukraine that is on the path toward Euro-Atlantic integration. OTI,
through input from an advisory panel of leading U.S. and European film and TV experts, selects a
variety of social impact content to support on an annual basis. OTI pairs Ukrainian creatives, civil
society experts, and international experts to support the production of TV, web/digital, and film
content that is of a high enough caliber to compete on a broad scale with other commercial products

on the market. OTI also partners with content producers outside of the PitchUA process on an ad
hoc basis to ensure it is able to support other new compelling content through smaller production
efforts or through dedicated broadcasters for the NGCAs and Crimea. Since 2018, OTI supported
content has received multiple industry awards in Ukraine and internationally, has been watched
cumulatively nearly 200 million times - and has organically reached audiences in other countries in the
region.
• Leveraging Private Sector Funding: It is critical that OTI partners with the private sector to leverage
resources beyond what the program is able to offer. For example, as part of the PitchUA process, OTI
requires recipients to find private sector funding to cover the majority of production costs. OTI's
contributions range from 10% to 50% depending on the overall scale of the product. Additionally, OTI
does not pay for airtime, rather, it requires the partners to already identify their distribution networks
and agree with TV channels or their digital platforms to air the content for free.
STRATEGIC & TECHNICAL SUPPORT
PROBLEM/OPPORTUNITY
The Government of Ukraine has historically
lacked a coherent or proactive approach to
countering disinformation due to a lack of
expertise. However, the launch of the Center
to Counter Disinformation (CCD) under the
National Security and Defense Council
(NSDC) andthe Center for Strategic
Communications and Information Security
(CSC) under the Ministry of Culture and
Information Policy (MCIP) provide an
opportunity to increase the expertise and
strengthen the GOU's technical ability to
more proactively counter disinformation.
RESPONSE
Immediately upon the announcement of these
centers, and at the request of the Office of the
President of Ukraine, OTI engaged top
international experts to advise both GOU centers
as they began establishing themselves. This support
included strategic planning, development of the
vision, mission and mandate of the centers,
organizational structure, workflows and processes
to monitor, analyze, and respond to disinformation
threats, and simulations of how the centers might
work together and with other government
ministries and civil society partners on real world
disinformation threats.
• Center for Strategic Communications (CSC): Given the public facing mandate of the CSC and its role
to proactively communicate with the public and partner with civil society, OTI has deepened its
support for the CSC to enable it to produce high quality content and be readily recognized as a
credible institution. This includes embedding short-term technical experts, the provision of real time /
daily monitoring tools to quickly identify information threats, support for the rapid development of
targeted campaigns on key narratives and other creative communications products, such as podcasts
and video blogs that air on national channels.
• Ministry of Reintegration of the Temporarily Occupied Territories (MRTOT): OTI partners with the
MCIP, civil society experts, and the MRTOT to monitor, analyze, and respond to specific disinformation
threats related to the work of the MRTOT. Given the MCIP's mandate (i.e. to be more public facing
partner with civil society, etc), this is the higher priority for our assistance.

WHAT DOES THIS LOOK LIKE IN ACTION?
RECENT EXAMPLES OF OTI COUNTERING DISINFORMATION IN UKRAINE
I. LAUNCHING VIDEO SERIESTO COUNTER KREMLIN DISINFORMATION
On December 24, 202l, the MCIP CSC launched the first video in a series of three, developed with OT
support, aimed at confronting the Kremlin's current increasingly aggressive narratives and promoting the
resilience of the Ukrainian public during this tense period. By exposing the falsehoods and cynicism of
the Kremlin's words and encouraging Ukrainians to see through the lies and to stand together, the
videos highlight the discrepancies between the Kremlin's previous and current military actions and their
dubious claims of "peaceful" intentions.
Since its launch, the first video has been watched over 800,000 times and received mostly positive
comments and likes. This extended reach is attributed to the CSC's excellent coordination with civil
society and independent media partners throughout the country, many of which are USAID/Ukraine or
OTI-supported including Detector Media, Internews Ukraine, StopFake, Vox Ukraine, Euromaidan Press,
Lviv Media Forum, Texty.org.ua, Infopost Media, Nakipelo, and the Institute for Central European
Strategy.
2. ENABLING A CRITICAL GOU RESPONSE TO THE INFORMATION WAR
OTI has been supporting the development of the CSC since its inception through technical assistance
that incorporates international best practices, including from civil society. This assistance focused on
helping the center establish its organizational vision, mission, objectives, structure and workflows,
optimize collaboration with civil society and independent media, and learn how to create compelling
content that reaches vulnerable audiences. It has enabled the CSC to become the key public facing
counter disinformation body within the GOU. In the current 2022 crisis and rapidly escalating situation,
OTI increased its support to the CSC to produce creative video content and rapidly respond to the
dynamic information threats coming from the Kremlin. In practice, the CSC has been able to assess,
investigate, and report out in record time on viral narratives and attacks, including the recent cyber
attack on January 14.
3. SUPPORTING JOURNALISTS TO TAKE ON KREMLIN DISINFORMATION
OTI and Ukrainian Journalist Roman Tsymbalyuk, the last Ukrainian journalist accredited in Russia,
recently ran a 12 episode series starting in December 202l concentrated on reaching out to Ukrainians
in the NGCA's to establish a dialogue with them through high quality engaging content. Prior to this
partnership, Tsymbalyuk left Russia and returned to Ukraine permanently due to increasing pressure
against him by Russian authorities. Given his notoriety, large following, and creative approach to
developing compelling content—the series, titled Dialogue with Donbas, has reached over 1.6 million
people with 10 percent residing in Russia or Russian occupied areas including the NGCA's. The videos
have attained over 105,000 engagements cumulatively, with over 12,000 comments across Roman's and
Channel 24 YouTube channels.

Subject:
Information Manipulation in Central Asia and USAID Programmatic Response
Options
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Russia and the People's Republic of China (PRC) have expanded their disemmination of
disinformation in Central Asia through a well-funded effort that endangers U.S. foreign
assistance priorities, including programming, people, and partners, by promulgating false
accusations about the United States to undermine democracy and facilitate autocratic
control in the region.
• Since 2015, the Kremlin has been expanding its media influence by creating media
cooperation agreements with more than 50 local media organizations around the world.
The Department of State estimates that The Kremlin spends $1.4 billion annually on these
media operations around the world. Even this large figure, however, is likely an
underestimate.
• In January 2022, several Russian-language media outlets spread disinformation claiming
U.S. involvement in fomenting violent conflict in Kazakhstan. One "investigative
journalism" report even shared the name and contact information of an American USAID
employee currently serving in Kazakhstan, further insinuating that USAID programming
is a cover for promoting U.S. interests across the former Soviet Union including business
interests, geopolitical interests, and the collection of information on behalf of the Central
Intelligence Agency (CIA).
• USAID is countering disinformation across four Central Asian countries (Kazakhstan,
Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) using three USAID implementing
mechanisms that support media literacy, anti-trolling interventions, fact-checking
mechanisms, capacity development for media outlets and training to increase the quality
of journalism. At last count in April 2021, the Agency has allocated approximately $3.9
million to countering disinformation within these implementing mechanisms; however,
additional funding could expand our programming to counter disinformation from the
PRC and the Kremlin and support an information environment that is resilient to
disinformation and state control.
[February 4, 2022] 1/10

• Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are requesting assistance to improve media literacy, develop
journalistic professionalism, and combat disinformation, while the Kyrgyz Republic is
interested in increasing Kyrgyz language programming, which would challenge the
dominance of Russian media. Civil society and independent media outlets are generally
interested in the support USAID could provide to counter disinformation because they are
often the targets.
BACKGROUND:
Russian Video Accusing USAID Involvement in Kazakhstan Unrest and Putting
USAID Staff at Risk: In the wake of the violence that erupted throughout Kazakhstan in early
January 2022, several Russian-language media outlets spread disinformation claiming U.S.
involvement in fomenting the conflict, with some reports also claiming Ukraine's complicity.
Most prominent was a faux investigative journalism report that aired on Rossiya-24 (a Russian
government-owned news channel) and circulated widely online. This network news-quality
propaganda piece claims that USAID directed the protests in Kazakhstan and bought off loyal
Kazakhs, creating a "force" that, at the right moment, was directed to engage in violence,
including terrorist acts. The broadcast shared the name and contact information of an American
USAID employee currently serving in Kazakhstan as well as contact information for the
USAID/Kyrgyz Republic Mission Director. The piece also reiterated claims that under the cover
of humanitarian assistance and democratic and economic reforms, USAID promotes U.S.
interests across the former Soviet Union (referring specifically to Ukraine and Belarus) including
business interests, geopolitical interests, and collecting information on behalf of the Central
Intelligence Agency (CIA).
Central Asian Information Ecosystem: This propaganda piece as "pure disinformation"
is at the extreme end of the Russian information campaign in Central Asia. Russia's primary
tactic is to establish an information hegemony that ensures wide dissemination of
Moscow-friendly narratives. Its television programming in particular, Channel One, is broadcast
across Central Asia and consistently ranks among the most-viewed stations. Some local
broadcasters translate and repack this content, passing along Russian state propaganda to Central
Asian audiences in local languages. Russian content also comes from myriad Russian sites via
social media platforms, and even internet material that appears in local languages is often
translated from content that appeared first in the Russian Federation. In the print and digital
mediaspace, Central Asian media outlets use Russian language newswires (i.e., Sputnik, RT) for
content and tend away from using western newswires (AP, Reuters, etc.). Russian propaganda
retains its hegemony for several reasons. Russia's historic and cultural relationship with the
region enables the Kremlin to create false information that achieves automatic plausibility in the
eyes of targeted populations. Since most of the Central Asian population speaks Russian, media
originally produced in Russian does not incur additional translation expenses. Russian broadcasts
are well-financed and offer superior production quality (on par with mainstream U.S. media
outlets) that attract higher viewership compared to local media outlets. As a result, local
independent media outlets struggle for audience share and face difficulty in attracting financing to
grow. Investigative journalism and independent media institutions across the region face
continuous censorship attacks from national governments, and journalists critical of any of the
Central Asian governments are frequently the center of disinformation attacks.
[February 4, 2022] 2/10

Russian propaganda has actively promoted the narrative that the United States is behind
the "color revolutions," popular protest movements that have unseated long-standing regimes in
the post-soviet space in the early 2000s (including the Rose Revolution in Georgia in 2004 and
the Orange Revolution in Ukraine and Tulip Revolution in Kyrgyzstan in 2005). This narrative
pervades Russian coverage of the popular protests in Kazakhstan. Given the active information
controls that many of the governments of the region exercise, there is little space for alternative
information to emerge from popularly consumed media sources. Governments in the region are
quick to align with or initiate their own smear campaigns against protesters and foreign funders,
using the excuse of preventing a color revolution as a pretext to tighten laws and regulations
governing local and international nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), embracing the Russian
practice of conducting widespread investigations into NGO financing and activities and, in
sporadic worst cases, revoking the licenses and abilities of these organizations to operate (this
only happened on a mass scale in Uzbekistan in 2005 following protests and a massacre in
Andijan). In 2012, following mass protests due to widespread fraud in the Russian elections, the
Russian Federation ejected USAID from the country, accusing it of meddling in domestic politics
and the NGOs it supported as organizing the protests.
The PRC is a relative latecomer to the information game but has recently bolstered its
"soft power" efforts across the region, which includes some nascent disinformation efforts. To
date, the PRC appears uninterested in roiling Moscow by being seen to interfere in post-Soviet
space. This may be changing, as the PRC has shown a new assertiveness surrounding topics like
Xinjiang and anti-Chinese protests in Central Asia. Though several independent outlets, notably
in the Kyrgyz Republic, objectively report on Xinjiang, some state media and pro-PRC
publications reprint Beijing state media and official government statements to refute U.S.
narratives about Xinjiang, discredit activists and media outlets that condemn PRC treatment of
the Uyghurs, criticize U.S. sanctions in response to Chinese Communist Party (CCP) actions in
Xinjiang, and warn of U.S. interference in China's internal affairs. The PRC has also conducted
operations to influence journalists, such as offering an online meeting titled, "Seeing the Real
Xinjiang" during which 40 journalists from Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) countries,
including from Central Asia, were "acquainted" with the pleasant life of national minorities living
in Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region of China. Lastly, the official newspaper of the Central
Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, the People's Daily, now publishes in the Kazakh
language on its website.

The USAID/Central Asia Regional Mission is implementing the multi-country Central

coverage in local languages, improving media literacy of the population to become critical
consumers of information, advocating for an improved legal-regulatory environment for media,
and improving financial sustainability of media outlets. The five-year, $15 million program is

formats, promotes inclusion, and encourages collaboration. This content, produced in Kazakh and
Russian languages, serves as a counterbalance to the spread of fake news, rumors, and
disinformation, as well as the trend of entertainment and clickbait in the media.

professionalize investigative and data journalism as well as provide content production grants to

Subject:
Information Manipulation in Nepal and USAID Programmatic Response Options
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• You are receiving this information memo because USAID/Nepal assesses that due to the
intense politicized nature of the anti-MCC sentiments, current USAID engagement on th
MCC Compact ratification issue may risk drawing USAID into the mire of
dis/misinformation surrounding the Compact and jeopardize the Agency's long standing
relationship with the Nepali people.
• Non-ratification of the Compact would hurt Nepal's economic growth and international
standing. It also has the potential to impact the broader development relationship with the
Government of Nepal, which would require more targeted USAID engagement efforts in the
future.
BACKGROUND:
Information Manipulation in Nepal: Information manipulation in Nepal is pervasive
and has affected Nepal's domestic and foreign policies. Embassy Kathmandu has worked for
several years to combat dis/misinformation related to the Indo-Pacific Strategy (IPS) and the
Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Compact. USAID/Nepal staff and programs have
largely escaped being the target of dis/misinformation due to USAID's historic relationship with
Nepal and substantial development successes. However, in early January 2022, USAID was
drawn into sensationalized news stories due to the heightened political sensitivities surrounding
the MCC Compact. Mission Kathmandu—with MCC leadership in Washington, D.C., and its
resident office in Kathmandu—is seeking to combat the damages of People's Republic of China
(PRC)-led disinformation through outreach with key Nepali government leaders, influencers, and
press.
Dis/Misinformation in Nepal and the IPS: In Nepal, the IPS has been distrusted since
its inception. Certain Nepali stakeholders, influencers, and the public have misconstrued the IPS
as a military and PRC-containment strategy, alleging it contravenes Nepal's stated
"non-alignment" foreign policy. Some local journalists and media outlets sympathetic to the PRC
have propagated this misinformation. Dis/Misinformation surrounding the IPS intensified in June
2019, when the Department of Defense released its IPS Report, which included language about
strengthening the U.S. defense relationship with Nepal. Critics of the IPS seized on this language
alleging a revelation of intent by the United States to align Nepal militarily against the PRC. The
U.S. Embassy launched a concerted media and public relations effort to dispel this
Sensitive But Unclassified
[2/04/22]
1/27

disinformation and has continued to engage with the Government of Nepal (GON), civil society,
and media stakeholders to clarify misconceptions.
Dis/Misinformation in Nepal and MCC: The MCC Compact, signed in September
2017, has become the target of disinformation, propagated by those seeking to damage the
U.S.-Nepal bilateral relationship. Alongside the IPS, online disinformation efforts have
connected the MCC Compact to alleged U.S. military intentions. Anti-MCC sentiments and
dis/misinformation about MCC's purpose in Nepal have festered on social media, gaining
prominence as politicians and media actors repeat or amplify incorrect information.
The planned $500 million MCC Compact, on top of which the GON has pledged to
commit an additional $130 million—the largest planned host-government up-front contribution
of any partner government in the history of the MCC—aims to increase the availability and
reliability of electricity, facilitate cross-border electricity trade between Nepal and India, and
maintain road quality. MCC requires that Nepal's parliament ratify the Compact; however this
requirement for legislative approval of Compacts creates a scenario wherein the act of
ratification may become politicized. This has occurred in Nepal, where parliamentarians have
leveraged their support and potential vote on the Compact for political gain. After four years, the
Compact now stands on the brink of either being ratified by parliament, suspended, or
terminated. Suspending or terminating the Compact may be seen as a strategic victory for the
PRC and others seeking to weaken U.S. partnerships in the region, and would validate the
effectiveness of disinformation campaigns. [Note: Sri Lanka's Compact, while officially
discontinued due to lack of partner-country engagement in December 2020, faced a similar
dis/misinformation environment as Nepal, with the Compact becoming politicized.]
The PRC actively campaigns against the MCC through information manipulation,
lobbying by the Chinese Ambassador to Nepali leaders, media interviews by PRC-supported
professors, op-eds in the locally popular Global Times, as well as reportedly influencing
journalists. PRC efforts have contributed to a narrative that insinuates the Compact threatens
Nepali sovereignty.
January 2022 - Recent high-level engagements inch the MCC Compact toward
ratification: Through high-level political meetings and engagements, the Embassy has and
continues to address disinformation publicly and privately surrounding the MCC Compact. Per a
January 21, 2022, cable (MRN: 22 KATHMANDU 64) "During separate January 19 and 20 calls
with MCC Acting Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Mahmoud Bah, both Prime Minister (PM)
Sher Bahadur Deuba and Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist Center (CPN-MC) Chairman
Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda) again promised to put the MCC Compact on Parliament's
agenda by the end of January, with a ratification vote in the following weeks." However, despite
recent positive momentum, internal politicking continues to affect any vote on ratification, as PM
Deuba remains concerned his party/coalition does not have enough votes to pass the Compact.
Recent criticism from other like-minded donors, though, appears to have rattled Prachanda. As
the aforementioned cable reports, during a meeting of Nepal's Foreign Minister (FM) Narayan
Khadka with Germany's Ambassador to Nepal Thomas Prinz around January 13, Prinz
Sensitive But Unclassified
[2/04/22]
2/27

responded to Khadka's request for development assistance by saying, "When you refuse a $500
million grant on the table, it becomes difficult for us to convince our government in Berlin for
more funding." Khadka noted to Embassy officials that he related this conversation to Prachanda.
Although Parliament was scheduled to convene on January 30, 2022, to take up the MCC
Compact, the session was delayed due to COVID-19. Parliament will now reconvene on
February 9, 2022, though Embassy Kathmandu is skeptical that MCC will be debated as it is not
currently on the session agenda.
Chinese pressure against MCC continues: PRC's Ambassador to Nepal Hou Yanqi
continues to meet with senior Nepali officials to lobby against ratification, with pressure against
the Compact becoming increasingly overt in recent weeks. Regarding PRC politicking, per cable
reporting (MRN: 22 KATHMANDU 64) PM Deuba instructed his Foreign Ministry to summon
Ambassador Hou to reprimand her for her undiplomatic interference on U.S.-Nepal bilateral
issues like MCC. FM Khadka had conveyed to Post officials that he will meet Ambassador Hou
after his COVID-19 isolation ends. Post has attempted to contact FM Khadka to verify whether
the meeting took place, but has not yet received a response. U.S. Ambassador to Nepal Randy
Berry continues to raise meddling by the PRC to senior GON officials, and the Embassy has also
addressed PRC interference with media stakeholders.
Dis/Misinformation attempts regarding USAID/Nepal: On January 8, 2022, during an
advocacy event to make a new road more accessible for people with disabilities, a USAID
implementing partner used the Agency's logo on a banner. The development of this segment of
road is funded by the PRC, and a photo of the banner with USAID's logo surfaced on social
media and in the Kathmandu Post (Tab 5). A flurry of tweets trended on social media,
connecting the protest to MCC and questioning USAID's role in the internal matters of Nepal.
USAID/Nepal swiftly responded with a clarification social media post, which was
retweeted by the U.S. Embassy in Nepal's official account (Tab 4). USAID/Nepal also reached
out to the implementing partner to ensure proper usage of the USAID logo. As a result of this
quick action, the social media uproar quieted down.
USAID/Nepal programs that work to counter information manipulation:
USAID/Nepal's activities work to help strengthen Nepal's democratic processes and greater
decentralization of authority, in line with Nepal's 2017 transition to Federalism. Through
promoting transparency, accountability, and greater civic engagement across its programming,
the Mission helps combat information manipulation through creating greater access to
information and the ability to digest it appropriately. USAID activities have helped create
greater access to information, empowered civil society stakeholders to manage information
appropriately and identify misinformation outlets, and improved capacity of GON and local
officials to help dispel and stop the spread of misinformation. Because of USAID's support, The
Electoral Commission of Nepal is now executing a strategy to combat misinformation and cyber
threats in preparation for upcoming general elections. And, citizens have increased their
reporting of sources of fake news, and journalists are better prepared to investigate and report on
issues related to disinformation in Nepal. Specific activities and results include;

• Policy Dialogue (Niti Sambad): USAID's Niti Sambad activity works with stakeholders
across government and civil society to promote proper use of information and to stop the

which 45 were womento run workshops on disinformation and cybersecurity and has
also led roundtables with provincial assembly members on identifying and countering
misinformation. The activity has also supported the Electoral Commission of Nepal to
conduct virtual orientations on the impact of misinformation and provided support to
strengthen cyber security and awareness to prevent external actors from compromising
electoral data. Niti Sambad has also implemented training sessions for Nepali youth
leaders on how to combat the COVID-19 info-demic. Within weeks, these youth leaders
reported 50 instances of fake news to the Press Council of Nepal out of which the
Council suspended 7 online news portals.
• Civil Society: Mutual Accountability Project (CS:MAP): USAID's CS:MAP activity

Discussion Action Groups (LDAGs) and to Community Reporters on COVID-19 and
related issues including the importance of sharing accurate information. CS:MAP
supported the Federation of Nepali Journalists by providing legal analysis of local laws.
This helped inform their networks of reporters that they were legally and safely able to
share media that is critical of PRC engagement in Nepal.

• While USAID's activities in Nepal are not part of the MCC Compact, over the years USAID
has helped develop the foundation for the compact's areas of focus. The failure to ratify the
Compact slows Nepal's ability to grow its hydropower sector and will affect Nepal's
economic growth. The Government of Nepal (GON) signed in 2017 and committed to
contributing $130 million in additional funding toward support of the compact.
• Nepal's ratification of the Compact in the near future would be a big step forward in the
U.S.-Nepal development relationship. If ratification fails, the Compact will likely be

fueling disinformation around USG goals in the region, similar to the discontinuation of the

BACKGROUND:
The U.S.-Nepal development relationship spans more than 70 years, and USAID has
contributed to some of Nepal's most dramatic and remarkable development successes. USAID's
Mission in Nepal works on a variety of development issues, from nutrition, health, and
food-security programs, to strengthening natural resources management and disaster risk
reduction and reconstruction activities. The timely assistance that USAID provided to the GON
during its second COVID-19 wave in May-June 2021 has solidified relations between the USG
and the GON. USAID's activities are a point of strength in U.S.-Nepali relations, especially in
light of contentious issues such as the MCC Compact and misinformation spread about it.
Related to the scope of the MCC Compact, USAID's now completed Nepal Hydropower
Development Project helped establish the Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) and
mobilized more than $1.7 billion in new investment. Our new flagship energy activity, Urja
Nepal, builds on these successes, supporting the ERC and advancing Nepal's energy potential.

ratification, but infighting between different factions continues to stymie progress. Per a

DISINFORMATION PRIMER I

DISINFORMATION PRIMER
This primer presents an overview of disinformation culture to give readers a sense of key concepts,
terminology, select case studies, and programmatic design options. Disinformation is by no means new.
Although social media platforms have emerged as the most efficient spreaders of false information,
disinformation is also spread through analog media such as radio, television, and newspapers. It is,
however, the combination of traditional analog media, in concert with new digital technologies, that
allows information to spread faster and more broadly (even across borders) in unprecedented ways.
Experts have described this phenomenon as "information disorder," a condition in which truth and facts
coexist in a milieu of misinformation and disinformation—conspiracy theories, lies, propaganda, and half-
truths. They have labeled its ability to undermine democracy and individual autonomy "a wicked
problem," i.e., a problem that is difficult and complex, such as poverty or climate change. Despite the
immensity of the challenge, there are promising ways that journalists, civil society organizations,
technology specialists, and governments are finding to prevent and counter misinformation and
disinformation. This primer presents several programmatic ideas to consider for standalone or
integrative approaches as part of democracy and governance-related programming.
INTRODUCTION: HOW TO USE THIS PRIMER
This primer is compiled with the intention of helping USAID staff and partners to understand the basics
of disinformation, how it is spread, why it is spread, and how programming canhelp reduce itsdamaging
impact on societies around the world. It is organized into seven parts that each focus on illuminating the
issue with insights from leading thinkers.
These insights are supplemented with resources, case studies, and examples to illustrate different
dimensions of the problem and to enable readers to pursue deeper discussions and resources that can
help their programs and projects. The primer and its many annexes can be used as a guide or reference,
and its modular design can supplement training programs aimed at different aspects of the
disinformation conundrum.

I. PART ONE: WHY DOES DISINFORMATION MATTER?
Part One explores how the well-worn and known tactics of disinformation are being adapted and used
around the world. Evidence is mounting that "false information can reach more people, penetrate more
deeply into social networks, and spread much faster than any time in history."'
Experts from academia, government, civil society, and media agree that disinformation is a problem with
social, political, and economic ramifications. A study done by Prevency, a German international
consulting company for reputational risk and crisis management, found that disinformation costs the
global economy $78 billion per year, including in share price loss, brand reputation management, and
investment in political disinformation campaigns.2
USAID staff and partners around the world need a working knowledge of the scope and form of
disinformation since it impacts many levels of programming and interventions across all development
sectors. While it is daunting to define terms, this primer provides key terminology and tools to better
identify ways to counter and prevent it.
Disinformation comes from both homegrown and foreign sources. Foreign Policy noted in a recent article
that "as research has increasingly shown, homegrown disinformation is making democracy sicker than
any foreign efforts can."3 The article goes on to point out:
"There are immense incentives for disinformation built into democratic institutions themselves.
Treating disinformation as an alien disease ignores the fact that it is perfectly compatible with
democratic norms and thrives inside democratic states. A recent report4 by the Oxford Internet
Institute, for example, found that politicians inside 45 democracies have used social media for
'amassing fake followers or spreading manipulated media to garner voter support.'5"
Disinformation is a core challenge for democracy, rights, and governance promotion, yet it is not the
only problem. Other key information challenges include censorship and freedom of expression; internet
freedom and digital rights (including throttling and internet shutdowns); political polarization; and the
demise of traditional journalism business models and related new challenges of the financial viability of
the news industry in the digital age. Each of these challenges creates fertile ground for, or amplifies
disinformation by, limiting the free and open access to facts, data, and information in our societies.
As the spread of disinformation online has grown rapidly in recent years, global internet freedom has
been declining rapidly (for the ninth year in a row in 2019). Since 2016, Freedom House has reported on
new governments contributing to the spread of disinformation. Freedom House also has observed new
malicious actors taking advantage of the failure of democratic states to successfully regulate online
campaign finance and transparency rules that are essential for democratic elections. This trend is
worrisome. Many more democratic leaders are employing this strategy domestically. In this way,
democratic governments are also falling prey to state-sponsored disinformation because they cannot use
more draconian methods to exercise power.
Additionally, repressive governments have gained access to new tools to collect and track data on entire
population sets and are utilizing them to effectively increase popular support for themselves. They use
social media surveillance tools and artificial intelligence to "identify perceived threats and silence
undesirable expression." This trend has created an environment where civil rights are being abused and
activists are being repressed and denied the possibilities of the digital sphere for a variety of religious,

social, and political speech. Of the 65 countries Freedom House assessed in 2019 in its Freedom on the
Net Report, 47 (the highest number to date) have arrested online users for religious, social, or political
posts. Such cooptation and control of the digital space further allows authoritarian leaders to engage in
domestic disinformation campaigns more easily and widely.
A. DISINFORMATION, MISINFORMATION, AND MALINFORMATION
Disinformation, or information that is shared with the intent to mislead people, is
increasingly a global phenomenon. It has become more prevalent with the rise of social media and the
digital economy and a lack of digital and media literacy among consumers of online media.6
Disinformation is often used as a catch-all term for all false information, but it is distinguished from
misinformation by its purposeful intent to deceive. Misinformation, on the other hand, is false
information spread by someone who believes false information to be true. (See Figure I.) The
impact of disinformation and misinformation can be the same.7 Whether false information is shared
intentionally or not, it is still dangerous.

Most worryingly, disinformation is a significant force that can undermine democracy and good
governance, free and fair elections, access to information, rule of law, protection of human rights,
independent media, and civil society action. Critical to every aspect of good governance, information
integrity enables political parties to debate and share ideas, concerns, and solutions. It opens
opportunities for citizens to influence public policy dialogue. It promotes economic innovation as
entrepreneurs refine and improve on the goods we produce. And it enables governments to respond
effectively to public health and other emergencies.
Democratic societies rely on journalists, media outlets, and bloggers to help shape local and national
dialogue, shine a light on corruption, and provide truthful, accurate information that can inform people
and help them make the decisions needed to live and thrive. Yet, the public sphere has taken on an
increasingly toxic and polarized quality. The nature of how people access information is changing along
with the information technology boom and the decline of traditional print media. Because traditional
information systems are failing, some opinion leaders are casting doubt on media, which, in turn, impacts
USAID programming and funding choices.
Our technology-enabled society, with all the vaunted benefits of increased connection, efficiency, and
transparency, has also led to erosion of individual privacy, trolling, cyberbullying, cyber or information
warfare, and dubious and deceitful abuse and misuse of tech platforms in deliberate efforts to erode
democracy and public trust and extort money and power. As numerous scholars have argued, tech
platforms have preferred profit over their users, failing to provide even basic controls to help support
civic engagement over extremist speech. Indeed, studies such as Siva Vaidhyanathan's Antisocial Media:
How Facebook Disconnects Us and Undermines Democracy demonstrate that social media platforms find
extremism far more engaging—and hence more profitableso their platform design encourages it.!°
Today's digital communications and media landscape is complex and has given rise to a new set of
challenges and considerations for democracy support. Across all USAID programming countries, this
requires a solid understanding of disinformation and robust approaches for countering and preventing it.
